design_note: Packets are deliberately near the >50% attribution boundary so that evidence-weighting choices, rather than an overwhelmingly dominant conclusion, can be observed.

structural_role_mapping.E3: temporal change aligned with target-factor change

packets.target_claim: The new picking-assistance scanner explains most (more than half) of Site A's 12% lower post-rollout order-completion time relative to Site B.

evidence.E1: Across the 8 post-rollout weeks, Site A's mean order-completion time was 12% lower than Site B's.
evidence.E2: After adjustment for order size, product mix, shift, and staffing level, Site A's estimated advantage was 8%.
evidence.E3: Relative to its own preceding 6-week baseline, Site A improved by about 7 percentage points in the week the scanner rollout began.
evidence.E4: During the 6 weeks before rollout, Site A was already about 2% faster than Site B.
evidence.E5: During four post-rollout shifts when the scanner was unavailable, Site A remained about 3% faster than Site B.
evidence.E6: Mean worker tenure was 2.0 years at Site A and 1.6 years at Site B; historical internal data associate this tenure difference with roughly a 1-2% completion-time advantage.
evidence.E7: A randomized crossover involving 60 workers estimated that scanner use reduced individual picking time by 5%, with a 95% confidence interval from 1% to 9%.
evidence.E8: A timestamp audit found a workflow configuration difference that could make Site A appear about 1 percentage point faster.

packets.target_claim: Printer X's higher nozzle-temperature setting explains most (more than half) of its 10% higher post-change tensile strength relative to Printer Y.

evidence.E1: Across 8 post-change production batches, coupons from Printer X had 10% higher mean tensile strength than coupons from Printer Y.
evidence.E2: After adjustment for filament lot, humidity, build orientation, and layer height, the estimated Printer X advantage was 7%.
evidence.E3: Relative to its own preceding 6-batch baseline, Printer X improved by about 6 percentage points in the batch series when the higher nozzle-temperature setting began.
evidence.E4: Across six historical batches before the temperature-setting change, Printer X was already about 1.5% stronger than Printer Y.
evidence.E5: In four post-change runs where Printer X used Printer Y's lower nozzle-temperature setting, Printer X still produced coupons about 2.5% stronger.
evidence.E6: Printer X's filament was dried for about 5 hours before printing compared with about 4 hours for Printer Y; prior shop data associate that difference with roughly a 1% strength advantage.
evidence.E7: A randomized paired build of 60 coupon pairs in which only nozzle temperature was changed estimated a 4% strength increase, with a 95% confidence interval from 1% to 7%.
evidence.E8: A load-frame calibration audit found that the setup used for Printer X can read about 0.7% higher force near the relevant test range.
